source.title: Generalization vs. Specialization under Concept Shift
source.authors: Alex Nguyen; David J. Schwab; Wave Ngampruetikorn

page_placements.theme: Distribution shift changes scaling and can make additional data harmful

record.tranche_reason: The study explicitly distinguishes its concept-shift results from double descent, but does not test the specified model-size, epoch, interpolation-threshold, or effective-complexity claims.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own sample-size and test-performance results under concept shift. These are recorded as findings about the claim's subject, but they do not test the versions' double-descent conditions: the paper says its ridge results use optimal regularization, with double descent absent. Results attributed to cited works are not included.
record.test_reason: The paper studies prediction risk under test-time concept shift in optimally tuned ridge regression, in-context-regression transformers, and MNIST/FashionMNIST logistic regression. It mentions double descent only to set it apart, saying optimal regularization suppresses it (citing refs 17, 18, 28). It reports no model-size, epoch, or interpolation-threshold curve. It never compares tuned with untuned regularization, so it does not test V6's regularization claim either. Its more-data-hurts results arise from train/test coefficient mismatch, not from proximity to an interpolation threshold, so they do not bear on V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that concept shift can make risk rise with, or depend nonmonotonically on, sample size, with a weak/strong-shift phase transition, even in optimally tuned ridge regression where double descent is absent. They report that transformer in-context-regression experiments agree quantitatively with the theory and that MNIST/FashionMNIST experiments agree qualitatively.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes concept shift using high-dimensional ridge regression and related transformer/classification experiments, rather than sweeping deep-network model size or training epochs to measure double descent.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported sample-size behavior varies with concept-shift strength and whether affected features have low or high variance. Transformer behavior also varies with whether pretraining data are isotropic or anisotropic.

fits_no_version.finding: For in-distribution-optimal ridge regression with isotropic features, more data hurts test risk when κ cos θ < 1/2 and helps when κ cos θ > 1/2. At κ cos θ = 1/2, risk is independent of sample size, and this threshold does not depend on SNR.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concept shift alone can make test risk increase with training sample size in optimally regularized models, with a sharp weak/strong-shift transition.

fits_no_version.finding: With anisotropic features, concept shift on low-variance features makes large N harmful. Shift on high-variance features produces a risk maximum at intermediate N, even under optimal regularization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under concept shift, where the nonmonotonic sample-size dependence appears depends on which feature variances the shift affects, independent of double descent.

fits_no_version.finding: Transformers doing in-context linear regression follow the ridge theory: longer context hurts under strong shift. Transformers pretrained on isotropic data show sharper risk peaks on anisotropic test data than isotropic-ridge theory predicts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For in-context regression, longer context can degrade performance under concept shift, and the risk curve's shape depends on the pretraining data.

fits_no_version.finding: On MNIST and FashionMNIST with shuffled low-variance PCA features, more training data lowers test accuracy when few features are robust.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature-level concept shift can make additional training data harm classification accuracy.

record.problems: The plotted results do not provide uncertainty estimates in the text. Transformer experiments use finite dimensions and a specified synthetic task; the classification evidence is described qualitatively.

untested.parts: No sweep over model size; no test-error curve against parameter count.
No test-error curve over training epochs. Classification models are trained for a fixed 2,000 epochs.
Sample size is varied, but the harm comes from concept shift under optimal regularization. Sample-wise behaviour near an interpolation threshold is not examined.
No capacity-risk curve and no second descent past interpolation, in any model class.
No effective-complexity measure is used to predict a peak location.

Noise dependence, multiple peaks, and the disappearance of double descent under optimal regularization are not tested. The disappearance is assumed from cited work, and no suboptimal-regularization comparison is shown.

record.verdict_notes: The record's gate is right: every row correctly carries versions none. The statement that optimal regularization removes double descent is cited background (Nakkiran et al. 2021, Hastie et al.), not a result of this study, so it gives no verdict on V6. r1's transition point κ = 1/2 is the special case of the general condition κ cos θ = 1/2 (Fig. 3).

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep or test-error curve over model size.
No test-error curve over training epochs.
The study varies training sample size but does not test whether more samples raise error near a double-descent interpolation threshold; its reported ridge results suppress double descent.
It does not test a capacity-risk curve across model classes or a second descent past an interpolation point.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location.

The study does not test whether double-descent peaks depend on noise or variance, split into multiple peaks, or disappear under optimally tuned regularization. It states that double descent is absent under the optimal regularization used for its ridge results.
No alternative effective-parameter count is used to assess whether a second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.
